findings.title: `caught_up` uses "tier configured" as its wanted flag while the status scope and the renderer's "n/a" text use "wanted range present"
findings.description: Description: In `_product_status`, `caught_up` is computed with `wanted=wanted_start is not None` (i.e. the tier is configured), but the actual `wanted` range can still be `None` when `entry.end` is unset and no `tick_dataset_edge` row exists, so `_scope` evaluates no wanted sessions. The renderer (`tick_status_render.py:101`) prints "caught up: n/a (no wanted range)" only when `caught_up is None`, so in that configuration the operator would see "caught up: no" with an all-zero bucket instead of the documented n/a state (the `caught_up` docstring in `tick_status.py` says "n/a when the product has no wanted range"). Today this is unreachable because `TICK_UNIVERSE` has `tier=None`; it will become reachable the moment slice 226 sets a tier with an open-ended range, and the two definitions could drift silently. Aligning `caught_up` with the same `wanted is not None` used to build `wanted` would make the "wanted" concept one value instead of two. No test currently covers the tier-set path at all, so the divergence has no guard.

findings.title: `calendar_sessions` duplicates the error-mapping of `product_session_days`
findings.description: Description: The new `calendar_sessions` in `tick_status_build.py` opens a `TradingCalendar`, calls `sessions_between`, maps `OperationalError`/`CalendarNotFoundError`/`OutOfPopulatedRangeError` to `TickCalendarError`, and closes the calendar — the same body as the existing `product_session_days` in `tick_calendar.py`, which differs only in that it derives the calendar id from the product and maps to `session_days`' touched-day set. Two spellings of "the calendar failed" now live in the package; if the exception set grows (e.g. a new calendar failure mode), the copies can diverge. The duplication is defensible — `calendar_sessions` returns `Session` objects, not days, and the callers have different needs — but it's worth collapsing into one shared helper in `tick_calendar.py` when slice 231 (GC) adds a second product and the pattern repeats.

findings.title: Read-verb exit-code behavior is well covered, including the documented 1-vs-4 asymmetry
findings.description: Description: The new CLI tests exercise the full matrix end to end: happy-path text and `--json` payloads for both verbs (JSON asserted equal to `build_coverage(...).to_dict()`), the mismatch → exit 3 path by deleting one primary-key row, preflight refusals (unknown `--product`, `end == start`) → exit 1, and an unreachable tick database → exit 4 for both verbs (verifying the `TickDatabaseUnreachable` override in `run_mapped` rather than the preflight path). Pure classification logic is unit-tested per-bucket with parametrization, and `raw_counts` is tested for rows crossing midnight and out-of-range rows. I list this only as the positive half of the review; the one gap is the one noted in the first finding (no tier-set path), not a defect in what is tested.

structured_findings.summary: `caught_up` uses "tier configured" as its wanted flag while the status scope and the renderer's "n/a" text use "wanted range present"
Read-verb exit-code behavior is well covered, including the documented 1-vs-4 asymmetry
